attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you brainstorm the functions that might be added to display each level’s tilemap on screen and to update each sprite’s properties on different types of tilemaps?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the structure of Red Belt Build activities differ from previous belts in IMPACT?

❓ What functions might be used to display each level’s tilemap on screen and to update each sprite’s properties on different types of tilemaps?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how the structure of Red Belt will differ from prior belts in IMPACT. In Red Belt, multiple Build activities across the level will be used to construct a larger, complex project based on a given theme (instead of multiple, individual projects). The starter code for each successive Build activity will be populated with code from the previous Build activity. At the end of the level, the ninja will have an opportunity to create their own complex project to add to their Red Belt portfolio, using theme-specific concepts applied throughout the Build activities.

💡 Prompt the ninja to brainstorm specific functions that might be needed to display each level’s tilemap on screen and to update each sprite’s properties on different types of tilemaps in this second Build activity. Encourage the ninja to write down ideas as pseudocode to think through the sequence and the logic of the mini golf code.
steps.instructions:
This is the second of three Build activities where you will create a mini golf project! 


Notice that the code from the Build 1 activity has already been added into the JavaScript editor. In this second Build activity, you’ll use that code to create multiple levels of the project. The mini golf course will contain 3 unique mini golf levels and the player will navigate between them using a top down tilemap.


What functions might be used to change how each sprite moves and interacts on the different tilemaps?

steps.hints: ❓ Did you test the sprite movement on the levelTwo and levelThree tilemaps?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice is different about the second and third level tilemaps, compared to the first? 

❓ What might the water and sand tiles be used for in each tilemap asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to open each of the tilemap assets and identify similarities and differences between each hole on the course. In the levelTwo tilemap, sand trap tiles are used to cause the ball to fall into them. In the levelThree tilemap, water tiles are used to cause the Ball sprite to revert to the beginning of the course. Both tilemaps have additional obstacles as well as starting and tee off and hole tiles.
steps.instructions:
Add the second and third holes of the mini golf course to the project!


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen and open the levelTwo and levelThree tilemap assets to be used for the second and third holes of the mini golf course. Like the levelOne tilemap, notice that each asset is longer than the width of the screen.


In the levelTwo tilemap, 2D sand tiles are used to create sand traps along the course. Notice where walls are removed so that the ball “falls” into the traps. 


In the levelThree tilemap, 2D water tiles are used to create water traps along the course. Notice where walls are added to the water tiles, so that code can be added when the Ball sprite hits one of the tiles.


Return to the JavaScript editor, then update the asset used in the setCurrentTilemap function to test each level on screen.


Click ▶ to test out each new hole on the mini golf course!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use multiple tileKindAt functions and OR operators to check for the tile image to the bottom of the Ball sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where can you find the names of the water tile assets?

❓ What happens when the Ball sprite overlaps a a water tile? 

❓Why is the code for the water tiles placed inside the onHitWall event?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to open the Assets menu, then find the 2D platformer water tiles (there are 3). The ninja can click on each tile to see the name, then copy the asset names and paste them into their code.

💡 When the Ball sprite overlaps a water tile, the camera will shake with a Ball sprite effect, and the Ball sprite will be placed back on the tee off tile.

💡 The code for the water tiles is placed inside the onHitWall event because there are multiple tile assets (left, right, and center) on the tilemap. This reduces the need to write this chunk of code 3 times.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Ball sprite lands in the water trap!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add another conditional inside the onHitWall event that checks if the tile to the bottom of the Ball sprite matches any of the water tile images.


If the tile to the bottom of the Ball sprite is a water tile, set the camera to shake and add a sprite effect to let the user know the ball has landed in water.


Then, use the after function to reset the Ball sprite’s position to the tee off tile’s coordinates and set its velocity to 0.


Update the tilemap asset displayed in the setCurrentTilemap function, then click ▶ to test out the water trap code!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the value of the topDown variable to match the current tilemap view in the callScene function definition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What does the topDown variable keep track of in the project?

❓ What code comments should be added inside the if/ else if conditional?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out the callScene function with different arguments to see different tilemap assets appear on screen. Scenes 0 (intro) and 3 (closing) will be added in the next build.

💡 The topDown variable will keep track of whether the top down tilemap is on the screen (navigating the golf course) or a 2D tilemap is on screen (playing a hole). In the next steps, the ninja will update each sprite’s movement, depending on which tilemap is on screen.
steps.instructions:
Add the top down tilemap to the project to allow the Player sprite to navigate between each level!


Declare a topDown variable set to true under // project initialization. This will be used to keep track of the current tilemap state.


Define a callScene function with a sceneNum number parameter to organize the scenes in the project. Inside the function definition, check if sceneNum is equal to 1 or 2.


If sceneNum is equal to 1, add a // top down comment as a reminder for what scene the project will display. Set topDown to true and display the topDownTilemap asset on screen.


If sceneNum is equal to 2, add a // 2D comment, update the value of topDown, then cut and paste the existing setBackgroundImage and setCurrentTilemap functions into the condition to display the levelOne tilemap asset.


Add a // project start comment to the editor, then call the function underneath, passing different arguments to test both scenes.


Click ▶ to display the top down and 2D tilemaps on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you pass different arguments to the callScene function definition to test the Player sprite’s code in both tilemap scenes?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might different properties be set for the Player sprite in the two different scenes?

❓ Does the Player sprite image and movement match the tilemap when different arguments are passed to the callScene function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that scene 1 is the top down tilemap (overview of the golf course). In this tilemap, the Player sprite should display a player image and be able to move in all directions of the tilemap, with the camera following. Scene 2 represents the 2D tilemaps of each hole. In these tilemaps, the Player sprite image should be set to the golf club, and the user should not be able to control its movement (this is coded separately by the Ball sprite and status bar). Its position should be set relative to the Ball sprite.

💡 Encourage the ninja to pass different arguments to the callScene function to make sure each function has been pasted in the correct place.
steps.instructions:
Update the Player sprite’s properties to match the current game condition.


Change the Player sprite’s starting image to the golfer image asset, which will be used to show the Player walking along the top down tilemap paths.


When the top down tilemap is displayed, reset the Player sprite’s image to the golfer image asset and allow the sprite to move with direction buttons to navigate to each hole. Place the sprite on the path tile in the top left corner of the tilemap and set the camera to follow.


When the 2D tilemap is displayed, set the Player sprite’s image to the clubImage asset and do not allow the sprite to move with direction buttons. Cut and paste the Player sprite’s existing setPosition code to place the golf club to the left of the ball.


Click ▶ to update the Player sprite’s properties depending on the tilemap displayed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Ball sprite’s Invisible sprite flag to true when the top down tilemap is displayed, and to false when the 2D tilemap is displayed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓Where should the Ball sprite’s code be placed inside the condition that checks if  sceneNum is equal to 2?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the Ball sprite’s code should be placed before the Player sprite’s in the scene 2 condition so that the Player sprite is placed correctly on screen.
steps.instructions:
Update the Ball sprite’s properties to match the current game condition.


Notice that the Ball sprite is still present when the top down tilemap is displayed. Use the Invisible sprite flag to only show the Ball sprite when the 2D tilemap is displayed. 


Then, cut the Ball sprite’s remaining code and paste it inside the condition that checks if  sceneNum is equal to 2 in the callScene function definition, to set its properties when the ball appears on the 2D tilemap.


Notice that the code creating the Ball and Player sprites need to remain outside of the function to act as a global variable, which can be accessed throughout the project code.


Click ▶ to test the Ball sprite’s update code in each tilemap scene.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a not operator to check if topDown is false inside the A button pressed and released events?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbol should be used to check that the top down tilemap is not on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use a NOT operator ! with the topDown variable to check that the top down tilemap is not displayed on screen.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The player and ball movement still function when the top down tilemap is displayed!


Inside the A button pressed event, check to see if the ball is not moving and if topDown is false before running the code inside the conditional.


Inside the A button released event, place all of the code inside a conditional that checks if topDown is false. 


Now, code will only run when the A button is pressed and released if a 2D tilemap is displayed on screen.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the A button is pressed and released on the top down tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you pass 1 to the callScene function definition to test the overlap code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What tilemap will be displayed when the Player sprite overlaps the horizStart or verticalStart tile assets? 

❓ What tilemap will be displayed after the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The 2D tilemap assets will be displayed when the Player sprite overlaps the horizStart or verticalStart tile assets on the top down tilemap. The top down tilemap will be displayed 2000 ms after the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the different overlap events to ensure that each tilemap asset appears when the corresponding tiles are overlapped.
steps.instructions:
Change the tilemap when certain tiles are overlapped!


Create 2 onOverlapTile events that make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps either the verticalStart or horizStart tile assets on the top down tilemap. Inside each event, call the callScene function to display the 2D tilemap.


When the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile at the end of each level, use another after function to display the top down tilemap again after 2000 ms, so that the user can see the Ball sprite disappearing into the hole, before ending the level.


Notice that scene 1 is called under // project start and then again after the Ball sprite disappears into the hole.


Click ▶ to test the code to begin and end each level.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Player sprite’s Invisible sprite flag to false when the top down tilemap is displayed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓When should the Player sprite’s invisible sprite flag be turned off?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to review the various sprite flags already in their code. Walk them through when the Ball sprite and the Player sprite should be invisible and when they should be visible on screen. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out their code, ensuring that the invisible sprite flags are turned off and on in the correct places.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player sprite is still invisible when the top down tilemap is displayed after the level.


Remember that the Player sprite disappears each time the ball is hit on the 2D tilemap. Add code to make the Player sprite visible again, once it has returned to the top down tilemap.


Click ▶ to test what happens after each level is completed.

steps.hints:
❓Did you nest 4 pairs of tilemap coordinates in the positionArray like this? 

[[#, #], [#, #], [#, #], [#, #]]
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbols should be used within and surrounding each element in the positionArray?

❓ Which coordinates should be added to the positionArray, so that the Player sprite can access each hole of the course?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that brackets need to surround each element (coordinate pair) in a nested array. Because each element contains x and y coordinates, a comma should separate the two number values. Additional commas should be placed between each element in the array, so that the code looks like: 

[[#, #], [#, #], [#, #], [#, #]]

💡 Prompt the ninja to open the topDownTilemap asset in My Assets to find the coordinates that the Player sprite should start on at the beginning of the project and after completing each hole of the course. It might be useful for the ninja to write down each coordinate pair, so that they don’t need to open the tilemap asset multiple times.
steps.instructions:
When the Player sprite returns to the top down tilemap, it’s placed in the same position and can only access the first hole!


Under // project initialization, declare a positionArray to store the coordinates to place the Player sprite on each time it returns to the top down tilemap. 


Open the topDownTilemap asset in My Assets and locate the coordinates that the Player sprite should be placed on at the beginning of the project, and after completing the first, second, and third holes. 


Store the coordinates in the positionArray by typing the column value, a comma, then the row value inside a pair of brackets, like this: [0, 0]. Add the remaining coordinates inside the array, separating the nested brackets with commas.

steps.hints:
❓ Did you pass the column and row coordinates at the levelNum index of the positionArray to the placeOnTile  function, like this? 

(positionArray[levelNum][0], positionArray[levelNum][1]))
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the levelNum variable keep track of in the project?

❓ What symbols are needed to access each element in the nested positionArray?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The levelNum variable keeps track of the current hole number for the mini golf course. This will place the Player sprite on a different tilemap coordinate when it returns to the top down tilemap. In the next step, the variable will be used to display a new tilemap asset on screen after the user has completed the previous hole.

💡 Walk the ninja through the code needed to access the elements in the nested positionArray. Remind the ninja that they should start by typing the name of the array inside the getTileLocation function, followed by two pairs of brackets. The first pair of brackets indicates the index of the element in the array. The levelNum variable should be placed inside the first pair of brackets to access each subsequent tilemap asset position. The second pair of brackets indicates the index within the element. The column coordinate will be stored at index 0 and the row coordinate will be stored at index 1.
steps.instructions:
Use a variable to keep track of the current hole number on the golf course!


Declare a levelNum variable set to 0 under // project initialization. Increase the levelNum variable by 1 whenever the Player sprite overlaps either the verticalStart or horizStart tile assets on the top down tilemap, before the next scene is called.


Update the Player sprite’s tilemap position when it returns to the top down tilemap. In the column parameter of the getTileLocation function inside the placeOnTile function, type positionArray followed by 2 pairs of brackets. In the first pair of brackets, type the levelNum variable, which will locate the pair of coordinates in the positionArray that match the current level. Then, type 0 in the second pair of brackets. This will locate the column coordinate (or the value at the 0 index) of the specified pair.


Then, copy the code from the column parameter and paste it into the row parameter. Change the value in the second pair of brackets to 1, to access the row coordinate of the specified pair.


Click ▶ to test where the Player sprite appears on the top down tilemap, after completing each level!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you subtract 1 from the levelNum variable to access the correct tilemap from the levelTilemaps array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the tilemap stored at the index 1 less than the levelNum variable value in the levelTilemaps array be displayed on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that arrays begin counting at 0. Because the levelNum variable value matches the number of the current hole on screen, 1 needs to be subtracted from its value to access the corresponding tilemap stored in the levelTilemaps array.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The project keeps displaying the levelOne tilemap at each hole!


Under // project initialization, declare a levelTilemaps array and store the three 2D tilemap assets inside.


Inside the callScene function definition, update the setCurrentTilemap function when a 2D tilemap is displayed. Use the levelNum variable to display the corresponding tilemap asset on screen to match each hole number. Remember that arrays begin counting at 0 and the levelNum variable is increased before the tilemap is displayed.


Click ▶ to test that the correct tilemap asset appears for each level!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the gameOver function to end the game once the Player sprite has completed all 3 holes?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What else might happen when the user completes all three holes of the mini golf course?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In the next build activity, the ninja will add a variety of customizations, including variables and splash screens, to make the project more engaging and improve the user experience.
steps.instructions:
End the game once the Player has completed all three holes!


Create an onOverlapTile event to end the game when the Player sprite overlaps the endTile asset on the top down tilemap. 


Click ▶ to try and complete the entire course!
